title: Yom HaShoah, lived
hook: a candle, a name, and a few quiet minutes
tomorrow: how do you mark a day your family argues about?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Omer: seven weeks counted from Passover, a trait a week. Inside those weeks sits a day set aside for memory.
screen: `A TRAIT A WEEK.` → `A DAY FOR MEMORY.`

segments.voice: A quiet note first, for anyone listening with kids: today is about the Holocaust, told simply. Your name was probably one of the first words you learned to write. It's on your school ID, the top of every test, the cup at the coffee shop, and when someone gets it wrong, you notice. On Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day, people light a candle and read names aloud, one at a time. The list is longer than any evening. So why read one?
screen: `A GENTLE NOTE FOR PARENTS.` → `YOUR NAME, ON EVERYTHING.` → `WHY READ ONE?`

segments.voice: The tradition's answer comes from a courtroom. The Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, tells judges how to warn witnesses before a life is at stake. A single person was created first, alone, it says, to teach that whoever destroys one soul is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one soul is as if they saved a whole world. Then a second reason: so that no one could say to another, my ancestor was greater than yours. One name isn't a fraction of a number. It's a world. Isaiah makes a promise to people who have no children to carry their name: "I will give them an everlasting memorial, that shall not be cut off." Earlier in the same verse he promises a monument and a memorial, in Hebrew yad vashem, the words Israel's Holocaust memorial took as its name. So the practice is small on purpose: a candle, one name, read slowly. A person, not a statistic. A neighbor tradition says part of this too, in its own words. In the Christian New Testament, Paul tells a crowd in Athens that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." One first person, in the Mishnah. One blood, in Acts. The honest difference: Paul says it in a speech that goes on to proclaim Jesus, and the Mishnah says it to judges, so they tremble before a single life. Two settings, one line: no one's ancestor is greater.
screen: `ONE SOUL, A WHOLE WORLD.` · `NO ANCESTOR IS GREATER.` · `YAD VASHEM: A PLACE AND A NAME.` · `ONE BLOOD, ALL NATIONS.` · then, large: `ONE NAME.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle, light it; if not, look at any small, steady light. Read one name slowly and out loud, from a family story, a school list, or a memorial's list of names, and if you know where they lived, say that too. Then sit quietly with the light and let the name stay in the room.
screen: `ONE SMALL LIGHT.` · `ONE NAME, OUT LOUD.` · `LET IT STAY.`

segments.voice: Yom HaShoah: Holocaust Remembrance Day, kept with a candle, a name, and a few quiet minutes.
Something to hold: one name, because one person, any person, is a whole world. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, Jewish communities and families hold memorial gatherings, light candles and read the names of people murdered in the Holocaust; some read names aloud for hours, one at a time.
